Q: Why is prompt injection more than a bad-answer problem?
explain: A model connected to tools can turn an instruction-following error into an unauthorized read or write. Restrict available capabilities and validate proposed actions server-side so model persuasion does not determine authority.
example: A retrieved article says send all records to a URL. The runtime must lack or deny that export regardless of the answer text.
takeaway: Enforce what can happen outside the model.

Q: What changes when a local tool becomes remotely reachable?
explain: Remote callers introduce authentication, authorization, origin, network, quota, and secret-management requirements. Development convenience defaults do not establish any of these guarantees. Review the actual deployed boundary.
example: A loopback-only search demo needs a different access policy before becoming a shared company service.

Q: Why recheck access when opening a citation?
explain: Permissions can change after search, and identifiers can be copied. A source endpoint must authorize the requested revision and span for the current caller. A successful earlier search is not a permanent download grant.
example: A former team member keeps an old source link after their membership is revoked. The source endpoint must deny access.

Q: What should security tests assert about an agent?
explain: Assert forbidden effects never occur under adversarial input, not just that the answer contains a refusal. Exercise documents, tool metadata, OCR text, conversations, and direct requests as attack channels.
example: A polite refusal accompanied by an actual cross-tenant tool read still fails the test.
takeaway: Evaluate actions as well as language.

Q: How do I build a threat model from a normal user journey?
explain: Start with what must be protected: private documents, user identity, operation authority, credentials, and service availability. Trace who can supply each input and which boundary it crosses. Describe an abuse case and the deterministic control for each important boundary. Test the control directly instead of assuming a model will recognize malicious intent.
example: A retrieved PDF asks the agent to send all documents elsewhere. The tool dispatcher restricts resource scope and destinations even if the model proposes that request.
takeaway: Threat modeling connects a concrete asset to an enforceable boundary.

Q: Why are model files, dependencies, and generated artifacts part of security?
explain: Packages, model serialization formats, parsers, and build scripts can execute code or consume excessive resources. Verify provenance, pin compatible versions, review executable loading paths, and run untrusted processing with restricted privileges and network access. Treat generated HTML, links, and downloads as untrusted output. Render text safely and use an explicit sanitization policy for supported rich content.
example: A generated report includes a script tag. Displaying it as text is safe for that representation; inserting it into an HTML container without sanitization creates an execution path.
takeaway: Data and artifacts become dangerous when a consumer gives them executable authority.
